data.title: THE ROAD TO JERUSALEM
data.subtitle: Outremer, 1189–1192
data.introBody: You are a Christian knight from Western Europe, sworn to the Cross and to your lord. The walls of Acre rise before you, stinking with siege and disease. Richard the Lionheart commands this host, but the Holy City is still a hundred miles away — and every mile will cost you something. Silver, sinew, or soul.
data.trailFeedOpener: The siege lines outside Acre, summer 1189. Heat, flies, and the smell of the dead.

events.title: The aftermath of Acre's fall — the day Richard orders the execution of the Muslim garrison and hostages on the plain outside the city walls
events.text: You stand in the line. The order has come down through every rank of command, lord to mesnie to you. The men beside you are moving forward. The prisoners — soldiers, yes, but disarmed, bound — are in front of you. Your confessor told you this morning that the King acts within his right; the ransom terms were broken, the Crusade cannot march on Jerusalem dragging three thousand captives. Your own lord, to whom you swore your sword in the sight of God, has passed you the command with his eyes. But you have been standing close enough to see faces. Both things are true at once. A knight next to you mutters that a man who sheathes his sword here will be remembered as a coward and an oathbreaker by every man who marches with him. You have until the trumpets sound.

choices.text: You move forward with the line. You do not look away. You are a knight under command in a holy war, and you do what your sworn duty requires.
choices.result: The knight has located his identity inside the chain of obligation — sacred oath, crusading purpose, and the solidarity of the host. What he does here is not separate from who he is; it is, from this moment, constitutive of who he is.

choices.text: You step back. You do not raise a hand against men who cannot defend themselves, whatever the command, whatever the cost to your standing among the host.
choices.result: The knight has placed his own witness — what he can and cannot be — above the oath-structure that orders his entire world. That act of refusal is not heroism in his own telling; it is a wound in every allegiance he holds, and he will spend the rest of the campaign living inside it.

events.title: Plague in the Trenches
events.text: Fever and flux are killing as many crusaders as Saracen arrows. A comrade in the next tent has collapsed. You have a small store of clean water and dried herbs — enough to help him, or to keep yourself sharp for the next assault.
trivia: Disease killed thousands of crusaders outside Acre — including Philip II's soldiers and members of the high nobility.
The garrison inside Acre was commanded by a resolute Ayyubid officer who held out for nearly two years before surrender.

choices.text: Share your water and herbs with him.
choices.result: He lives another week. He remembers you did not pass by.

choices.text: Keep your stores. You must stay battle-ready.
choices.result: You stay healthy. He is carried out of the tent by morning.

choices.text: Report it to the camp surgeon and let him decide.
choices.result: The surgeon is overwhelmed. He nods and moves on. Your comrade's fate is the same.

events.title: Philip Sails Home
events.text: Acre has fallen, but Philip II of France announces he is returning to France — taking his household knights and a portion of the French infantry with him. Your lord is furious. Philip leaves behind the Duke of Burgundy to command the remaining French troops, but the coalition is visibly cracking.
trivia: Philip II left the Holy Land in August 1191, shortly after Acre's surrender, citing illness and political threats at home.
His departure forced Richard to reorganize the entire crusader order of march for the coastal advance.

choices.text: Argue openly that Philip's departure dishonors France.
choices.result: Several knights nod. The Duke of Burgundy looks at you coldly. You have made an enemy worth watching.

choices.text: Say nothing. Swallow it and adapt.
choices.result: A prudent silence. The army re-forms without drama from you. The wound is still there.

choices.text: Volunteer to go with Philip. You miss home.
choices.result: Your lord's eyes follow you across the camp for a long moment. You see what it costs you in his face.

events.title: The March to Jaffa
events.text: Richard orders the army south along the coast toward Jaffa in tight formation — crossbowmen on the seaward flank, knights inside, no one breaks ranks regardless of provocation. Saladin's horsemen ride close, hurling javelins and arrows, trying to goad a charge. The discipline is brutal and the heat is killing.
trivia: Richard's coastal march was disciplined by design — the fleet kept pace offshore, supplying the army and preventing encirclement.
Saladin's forces tried repeatedly to provoke the crusaders into breaking formation before Arsuf.

choices.text: Hold the line. Endure the arrows.
choices.result: You take two arrows in your shield and do not move. Richard notes the steadiness of your rank.

choices.text: Break and charge. You can end this harassment.
choices.result: Richard's officers drag you back with fury. You cost the army a planned formation and nearly your horse.

choices.text: Drift toward the center — less exposed.
choices.result: You avoid the worst of the arrows. Others notice you are not where you were posted.

events.title: Conrad or Guy?
events.text: Your lord summons you to a council meeting. Conrad of Montferrat and Guy of Lusignan both claim the crown of Jerusalem, and their factions are nearly coming to blows in the camp. Your lord asks which man you think Richard should back — and tells you your word will carry weight with him.
trivia: The dispute between Conrad of Montferrat and Guy of Lusignan divided the crusader leadership throughout the campaign.
Conrad had defended Tyre against Saladin in 1187 when most of the kingdom fell — a fact his supporters never let the army forget.

choices.text: Back Conrad. He held Tyre when others fled.
choices.result: Your reasoning is heard. Conrad's faction nods. Guy's men watch you narrowly for the rest of the campaign.

choices.text: Back Guy. Richard favors him; backing Guy costs nothing.
choices.result: Your lord is pleased. You receive a small gift of silver. You know what you traded for it.

choices.text: Say it is not your place to judge kings.
choices.result: A safe answer. Your lord dismisses you without expression.

events.title: A Brother in Saracen Hands
events.text: Word comes that a knight from your mesnie — a man who shared your fire from the beginning — has been captured near Jaffa. His Ayyubid captors demand ransom: twenty silver pieces, enough to dent your purse badly. Your lord will not pay it; he says the man should have been more careful.
trivia: Ransom was a common medieval practice — captured knights were often held for payment rather than killed.
Saladin was noted by both Christian and Muslim sources for releasing some prisoners without ransom, though this was not always the policy of his commanders.

choices.text: Pay the ransom yourself.
choices.result: He walks back into camp three days later. He owes you a debt he will spend years repaying. Your purse is light.

choices.text: Raise half and ask the mesnie to cover the rest.
choices.result: The mesnie grumbles but contributes. He comes home. The bond between you all is tighter for the cost.

choices.text: Leave it. Your lord is right — you cannot afford it.
choices.result: He is never heard from again. Men in the mesnie remember who did not reach for their purse.

events.title: The Road Stops Here
events.text: Richard has halted the march. The council says Jerusalem cannot be held even if it is taken — the crusaders must go home, and Saladin's forces are too strong. Richard is negotiating a treaty. You may accept, take your silver, and sail. Or you may refuse to leave, joining a small company of knights who swear to stay and garrison what remains of the crusader coast, knowing they may never see home again.
trivia: The Treaty of Jaffa in September 1192 ended the Third Crusade — Christian pilgrims were granted safe access to Jerusalem, but the city itself remained under Saladin's control.
Richard never entered Jerusalem. He reportedly turned away from a hilltop where he could have seen the city, saying he was not worthy to enter what he could not retake.

choices.text: Stay. Someone must hold the coast.
choices.result: You watch Richard's fleet sail. The coast is cold and the garrison is thin. You made an oath to something larger than yourself. You will keep it as long as you can stand.

choices.text: Accept the treaty and sail home.
choices.result: The sea carries you west. Three years of memory cross with you. Your family will not know your face has changed. You do not know yet how much you left behind.

choices.text: Wait to see what the other knights do, then follow.
choices.result: You trail the majority onto the ships. The decision was made for you. The coast disappears behind the fleet.

events.title: Before the walls of Jerusalem — the Crusade has stalled in council, leaders argue, and a captured Saracen scout is brought before your lord for questioning under duress. Your lord looks at you.

text.default: Your lord does not need to speak. You stepped forward at Acre; the shape of who you are in this army was decided there. You feel it not as reluctance but as something heavier — a recognition. You have already chosen what instrument you are willing to be. The scout's eyes find yours, and you do not flinch, and that is the most terrible thing: that you no longer have to decide.

variants.text: Your lord does not need to speak. You stepped forward at Acre; the shape of who you are in this army was decided there. You feel it not as reluctance but as something heavier — a recognition. You have already chosen what instrument you are willing to be. The scout's eyes find yours, and you do not flinch, and that is the most terrible thing: that you no longer have to decide.

Your lord's eyes carry what they have carried since Acre — the knowledge of what you would not do. He does not ask you. He looks past you to another man, and the slight is as precise as a blade. You watch from the edge of the circle, and the isolation you chose at Acre is here again, complete. You tell yourself you are still a knight. You are not entirely sure the men around you agree, and you are not entirely sure, standing here, that your refusal bought the thing you hoped it would.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Richard I of England
sages.title: The Lionheart — Commander of the Crusade
sages.bio: Richard I led the Third Crusade after taking the cross in 1187. A gifted battlefield commander, he drove the siege of Acre to conclusion and won the Battle of Arsuf, but political complications and the impossibility of holding Jerusalem forced him to accept a treaty rather than retake the Holy City.
sages.greeting: The king rides down the siege line at dusk, inspecting the earthworks himself. He stops his horse beside you and looks at the walls.
sages.advice: "Every foot of ground outside those walls is bought with a man's suffering. Do not waste it on bad discipline or worse politics."

question.question: Why did Richard accept a treaty with Saladin in 1192 rather than fight on for Jerusalem?
choices: He had been bribed by Saladin's gold
Even if taken, Jerusalem could not be garrisoned and held
The Pope ordered him to stop fighting
Saladin's army had already abandoned the city
question.explanation: Richard's council argued that the crusading army lacked the men to hold Jerusalem after capturing it — Saladin could retake an under-garrisoned city almost immediately. Taking the city without the means to hold it would have been a hollow victory.
question.teksRef: 7.2(A) — Political and military developments of the Crusades

sages.name: Saladin
sages.title: Sultan of Egypt and Syria — Defender of Jerusalem
sages.bio: Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub unified Egypt and Syria under Ayyubid rule and recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 at the Battle of Hattin, triggering the Third Crusade. Known in both Muslim and Christian sources for strategic brilliance and occasional acts of mercy, he ultimately secured Jerusalem through the 1192 treaty.
sages.greeting: A captured Ayyubid officer who speaks Frankish is brought to your camp. He does not flinch when he speaks of his lord.
sages.advice: "He does not hate your faith. He defends a city. You would do the same. The question is what you are willing to become in order to take it."

question.question: What event in 1187 triggered the calling of the Third Crusade?
choices: Saladin conquered Egypt and founded the Ayyubid dynasty
Saladin defeated the crusaders at Hattin and retook Jerusalem
The Byzantine Empire fell to Muslim forces
Conrad of Montferrat surrendered Tyre to Saladin
question.explanation: At the Battle of Hattin in July 1187, Saladin destroyed the main crusader army and captured King Guy of Lusignan. Jerusalem fell in October 1187. These events shocked Christian Europe and prompted Pope Gregory VIII to call the Third Crusade.
question.teksRef: 7.2(A) — Causes and context of the Third Crusade

sages.name: Crusader Foot Soldier
sages.title: Common Infantry of the Third Crusade
sages.bio: The rank and file of the crusading army — pilgrims, levied infantry, and household crossbowmen — endured disease, heat, starvation, and battle without the armor, horses, or political standing of knights. Their endurance during the coastal march made Richard's strategy possible.
sages.greeting: A haggard infantryman limps into your camp and sits down without asking. He has an arrow scar across his collarbone and says nothing for a long time.
sages.advice: "We held the march because we had orders and because the man next to us held. That is all. Do not make it more than it was."

question.question: What was Richard's main reason for keeping the army in tight marching formation along the coast?
choices: To show off his army's discipline to local Christian populations
To prevent Saladin's cavalry from breaking the column and scattering the crusaders
To keep the fleet in sight for navigation purposes
To allow the sick and wounded to keep pace at the rear
question.explanation: Richard's tight formation denied Saladin's faster cavalry the gaps they needed to shatter the column. Breaking formation to pursue harassing riders was exactly the trap Saladin was setting — Richard's orders held the army together through weeks of provocation.
question.teksRef: 7.2(B) — Military strategy and tactics of the Third Crusade

route.title: The Crusade, 1189–1192
route.description: From the siege trenches of Acre to the road that ends short of Jerusalem.

eventTrivia.question: What city did the crusaders besiege for nearly two years before it surrendered in 1191?
choices: Jerusalem
Jaffa
Acre
Tyre
eventTrivia.fact: Acre was besieged from 1189 and fell to the crusaders in July 1191 — the Third Crusade's first major victory.

eventTrivia.question: Which European king left the Holy Land shortly after Acre fell, weakening the crusader coalition?
choices: Richard I of England
Philip II of France
Frederick Barbarossa
Guy of Lusignan
eventTrivia.fact: Philip II of France sailed home in August 1191, citing illness and disputes at home, leaving Richard in sole command.

eventTrivia.question: What agreement ended the Third Crusade in September 1192?
choices: The Peace of Westphalia
The Treaty of Jaffa
The Concordat of Acre
The Truce of Tyre
eventTrivia.fact: The Treaty of Jaffa allowed Christian pilgrims safe access to Jerusalem while the city itself remained under Saladin's control.

eventTrivia.question: What happened at the Battle of Hattin in 1187 that triggered the Third Crusade?
choices: Frederick Barbarossa drowned crossing a river
Conrad of Montferrat surrendered Tyre
Saladin defeated the crusaders and retook Jerusalem
Philip II refused to send reinforcements
eventTrivia.fact: Saladin destroyed the main crusader army at Hattin and captured Jerusalem in October 1187, shocking Christian Europe into launching the Third Crusade.

eventTrivia.question: Why did Richard's council advise against a final assault on Jerusalem?
choices: The army had run out of siege equipment
They lacked enough men to garrison and hold the city after taking it
Saladin had offered a higher ransom than expected
The Pope had forbidden any further bloodshed
eventTrivia.fact: The council argued that capturing Jerusalem without the strength to garrison it would be pointless — Saladin could retake an undefended city almost at will.

eventTrivia.question: Who defended Tyre against Saladin in 1187 when most of the crusader kingdom fell?
choices: Guy of Lusignan
Richard I
Conrad of Montferrat
Philip II of France
eventTrivia.fact: Conrad of Montferrat arrived at Tyre and organized its defense, holding it as the last major crusader port after the fall of Jerusalem.

eventTrivia.question: What did Richard's coastal march discipline require soldiers to do despite Saracen harassment?
choices: Charge the enemy cavalry on sight
Hold formation and not break ranks
Retreat to the fleet each night
Fight only at night to avoid the heat
eventTrivia.fact: Richard's orders forbade breaking formation even under arrow fire — Saladin's cavalry was trying to goad a charge that would scatter the crusader column.

eventTrivia.question: How did disease affect the crusaders outside Acre?
choices: It had almost no effect because the army was well-supplied
It killed thousands, including noble commanders, before the city fell
It only struck the Saracen garrison inside the walls
It was contained quickly by crusader physicians
eventTrivia.fact: Fever and dysentery devastated the besieging army — including high nobles and members of Philip II's retinue — making the siege as much a war of attrition against disease as against the garrison.

eventTrivia.question: What role did the fleet play in Richard's coastal march from Acre to Jaffa?
choices: It carried the cavalry horses so the knights could rest
It kept pace offshore, supplying the army and preventing encirclement
It blockaded Saladin's ports to cut off Ayyubid reinforcements
It had no role — the army marched entirely inland
eventTrivia.fact: The fleet shadowed the army along the coast, resupplying it and guarding the seaward flank, which was central to Richard's strategy for reaching Jaffa intact.

eventTrivia.question: What dispute between crusader leaders threatened to split the army throughout the campaign?
choices: A feud between English and German knights over looting rights
Conrad of Montferrat and Guy of Lusignan's rival claims to the crown of Jerusalem
A disagreement between Richard and his own brother over command
Philip II's demand to command the siege artillery
eventTrivia.fact: Conrad of Montferrat and Guy of Lusignan both claimed the throne of Jerusalem, and their competing factions created dangerous divisions in the crusader command structure throughout the campaign.

eventTrivia.question: What was the common medieval practice when a knight was captured in battle?
choices: He was executed immediately as a prisoner of war
He was held for ransom and released when payment was made
He was forced to convert to his captor's religion
He was enslaved and put to work in the fields
eventTrivia.fact: Ransom was a standard practice in medieval warfare — captured knights were valuable property, and both sides regularly exchanged prisoners for payment.

eventTrivia.question: What did Saladin's forces attempt during the crusader coastal march to break the army?
choices: They flooded the coastal road with diverted river water
They repeatedly harassed the column with cavalry to provoke a charge and break formation
They blockaded the fleet to cut off the army's supplies
They sent envoys offering false truces to slow the advance
eventTrivia.fact: Saladin's cavalry rode close, hurling javelins and arrows, hoping to goad crusader knights into breaking formation for a charge — which would have exposed the whole column to destruction.

eventTrivia.question: Richard reportedly turned away from a hilltop overlooking Jerusalem without entering. Why?
choices: He was afraid of Saladin's garrison inside the walls
He said he was not worthy to see what he could not retake
His horse was injured and he could not make the climb
Philip II had forbidden the advance without French troops
eventTrivia.fact: According to the sources, Richard refused to look upon Jerusalem from the hilltop, saying he was not worthy to behold what he could not deliver to Christendom.

eventTrivia.question: What did the Treaty of Jaffa grant Christian pilgrims?
choices: Control of Jerusalem and its holy sites
Safe passage to visit Jerusalem, which remained under Saladin's rule
A permanent crusader garrison inside Jerusalem's walls
The return of all prisoners taken during the campaign
eventTrivia.fact: The Treaty of Jaffa gave Christian pilgrims the right to travel safely to Jerusalem and visit its shrines, but the city itself stayed under Saladin's control — the crusade's central military goal was not achieved.

eventTrivia.question: What was the oath a knight swore when he took the cross?
choices: To obey the Pope in all political matters
To travel to the Holy Land and fight to defend or recover it
To give half his property to the Church before departing
To never accept ransom if captured by Saracens
eventTrivia.fact: Taking the cross meant swearing a formal vow to go on crusade — a sacred pilgrimage obligation that bound the knight to fight for the Holy Land under pain of spiritual penalty if he abandoned it.

eventTrivia.question: How did Saladin's unified Ayyubid state differ from the crusader coalition Richard commanded?
choices: Saladin had a much larger army but worse siege equipment
Saladin commanded a single unified state; Richard led a coalition of rival European lords and factions
The Ayyubid army relied entirely on naval power while the crusaders had none
Saladin's forces were mostly volunteer pilgrims, like the crusaders
eventTrivia.fact: Saladin ruled Egypt and Syria as a single system with unified command and logistics. Richard led a coalition of English, French, and other European lords whose rivalries — like the Conrad-Guy dispute — constantly threatened to fragment the army.

data.historicalContext: The Third Crusade (1189–1192) was called after Saladin's decisive victory at the Battle of Hattin in 1187 and the subsequent fall of Jerusalem. Richard I led the most organized Christian response, capturing Acre in 1191 and defeating Saladin at Arsuf and Jaffa — but the coalition never had the strength to hold Jerusalem even if it could be taken. The campaign ended with the Treaty of Jaffa: Christian pilgrims could visit Jerusalem, but the city remained under Ayyubid control. Richard sailed home in October 1192. Saladin died in 1193, having held what he had won. The crusader states lingered for another century on the coast, but Jerusalem would not be under Christian rule again until the twentieth century.

verdict.good: You came to Outremer with an oath and you kept it past the point where keeping it cost you. Not every man in that army can say that. The Crusade failed its central purpose — Jerusalem stayed in Saladin's hands, Richard sailed, Debs — no, Debs was someone else. Richard sailed in October 1192. The city you marched toward never opened its gates to you. But you stood in the line when the line held, you paid out of your own purse when no one made you, and you stayed when the ships left. History will not record your name. It will record that some knights did not leave. You were one of them.
verdict.bad: You made the calculation every time. Philip's departure, the march, the ransom, the final question at the shore — each time you found the exit and took it. That is not weakness. It is a kind of discipline. But the men who paid the ransom and held the formation and stayed after the fleet sailed were standing next to you the whole time, and you saw what they chose, and you chose differently. Jerusalem was not retaken. The treaty gave pilgrims safe passage to a city that remained under Saladin. You sailed home with your silver and your condition intact. The cost was carried by others. You knew that. You went anyway.
verdict.indifferent: You were there. That is the true and complete account of your presence in this war. The siege lines, the march, the council tent where a crown was disputed — you stood in all of it and waited for someone else to make it mean something. The Third Crusade failed its purpose and Saladin kept Jerusalem, and you passed through the whole of it without it asking anything of you, because you never offered anything. A knight is defined by what he is willing to stand for when standing is costly. Three years of holy war and you are still waiting to find out what that is.

data.reviewSummary:
The Third Crusade began because of a catastrophe. At the Battle of Hattin in July 1187, Saladin — the Ayyubid Sultan of Egypt and Syria — destroyed the main crusader army and captured King Guy of Lusignan. Jerusalem fell to Saladin's forces in October 1187. The shock in Christian Europe was immediate: Pope Gregory VIII called a new crusade, and the kings of England and France took the cross.

The siege of Acre lasted from 1189 until July 1191, when the city's Ayyubid garrison finally surrendered. Disease killed thousands of crusaders in the siege camps — including high nobles — before a single wall was breached. The garrison commander held out for nearly two years, and the fall of Acre was the crusade's first great test of endurance, not just valor.

Shortly after Acre fell, Philip II of France sailed home in August 1191, citing illness and political threats in France. He left the Duke of Burgundy to command the remaining French troops, but his departure weakened the coalition Richard now led alone. The dispute between Conrad of Montferrat — who had defended Tyre when the rest of the kingdom fell — and Guy of Lusignan over the crown of Jerusalem created dangerous divisions that followed the army south.

Richard's coastal march from Acre to Jaffa succeeded because he held his army in strict formation despite relentless harassment from Saladin's cavalry, who were trying to goad a charge and break the column. The fleet kept pace offshore, supplying the army and guarding the seaward flank throughout the march.

Richard won battles but could not win the war. His council warned that even if Jerusalem were taken, the army lacked enough men to garrison and hold it — Saladin could retake an undefended city at will. Richard reportedly turned away from a hilltop where he could see Jerusalem, saying he was not worthy to behold what he could not retake.

The campaign ended with the Treaty of Jaffa in September 1192. Christian pilgrims received the right to travel safely to Jerusalem and visit its holy sites, but the city itself remained under Saladin's control. Richard sailed home in October 1192. Saladin died the following year. Jerusalem would remain under Muslim rule for centuries.

data.title: DUST AND DISTANCE
data.subtitle: Oklahoma Panhandle to California, 1935
data.introBody: Summer, 1935. The bank notice is nailed to the door. The truck is loaded. You have a little cash from selling the furniture and the mule, a crate of home-canned goods, and a battered 1928 flatbed that is your only way west. Every mile, every roadside camp, every dollar spent on gas or a doctor brings you closer to California — or closer to nothing.
data.trailFeedOpener: Summer 1935: the notice is on the door and the truck is backed up to the porch.

events.title: The Notice Morning
events.text: The bank's sheriff has tacked a dispossession notice to the door post. Dust is banked against the barn. Your youngest has a rag tied over her face to breathe. Your father-in-law sits on the porch rocker and will not look at the notice. Your husband has already backed the truck to the door and is asking you — you, not him — to say the word, because he cannot say it himself. Two neighbors came at dawn: one to say a cousin in Bakersfield has work, one to say that three families on the next section stayed and the rains came back last April for a week. The truck holds one load. You have until sundown before the bank's man returns with a deputy.

choices.text: Tell your husband to start loading. You walk to your father-in-law, take his hands, and say: 'Papa, we are going. Help me choose what comes with us.' You do not look back at the graves behind the barn.
choices.result: The player has chosen the family of the living over the family of the dead and the soil — they are someone who can sever when severing is the only way forward, and who carries the cost of that severance inward rather than outward.

choices.text: Tell your husband to put down the truck keys. You walk to the bank notice and pull it from the post. You say: 'We work this land. We are not leaving it for a piece of paper.' You send the neighbor with California news away and ask the other one about last April's rain.
choices.result: The player has chosen the claim of place over the claim of possibility — they are someone who measures a family's worth by what it will not abandon, and who would rather be defeated on ground they know than dissolved in ground they don't.

events.title: Radiator Gone Dry
events.text: The truck shudders and steam hisses up from under the hood on a stretch of New Mexico hardpan. The radiator is dry. A man in a rusted pickup stops and offers you a jug of water — for a price, or as a gift if you ask straight.
trivia: Overheated radiators were one of the most common breakdowns on Route 66 in the 1930s.
Migrants carried extra water jugs because desert stretches had no service stations for miles.

choices.text: Pay him what he asks. Fix it fast.
choices.result: The jug saves you. The engine cools and you're rolling again. But four dollars is a day's wages you won't see back.

choices.text: Ask straight — tell him you're short.

outcomes.result: He hands it over free. 'I was on the road last year,' he says. You pour the water and don't look back.
He softens some but wants a little something. Two dollars. The truck cools enough to limp to the next town.

choices.text: Wait him out. He'll give it free.

outcomes.result: He shrugs and pours the jug. You saved the money but you can feel the silence between you.
He drives off. You sit in the sun two hours before another car stops — and that one charges double.

events.title: Cotton by the Acre
events.text: A labor contractor is parked at the crossroads with a hand-lettered sign: pickers wanted, fifty cents per hundred pounds. It is a day lost, maybe two. But the cash is real and the family is hungry.
trivia: Migrant families often stopped to pick cotton or fruit to replenish cash before reaching California.
Labor contractors in the Southwest paid piece-rate wages that rarely covered a family's daily costs.

choices.text: Stop and pick. Two days' work.
choices.result: The children fill sacks alongside you. It is hard work and bad pay but the larder is fuller and the kids are not crying tonight.

choices.text: Negotiate for better pay first.

outcomes.result: He haggles you down to sixty cents per hundred. Better than nothing. The family eats.
He waves you off. 'Next family'll take the fifty cents.' You drive on hungrier than before.

choices.text: Keep driving. California has better work.
choices.result: You press on. The children ask when they'll eat a real meal and you tell them soon. You hope you're right.

events.title: Broke Down on the Shoulder
events.text: A family with Oklahoma plates sits on the shoulder, hood up, three kids in the truck bed. Their axle is cracked. They look like your cousins. They need a tow into town and a few dollars for the part.
trivia: Dorothea Lange's photographs for the Farm Security Administration documented exactly these roadside breakdowns, putting a human face on the migration for the American public.
The FSA, part of Roosevelt's New Deal, hired photographers to document rural poverty and build support for federal relief programs.

sageAdvice.name: Dorothea Lange
sageAdvice.line: Every family I photograph on this road is the same story: the land failed them before they failed the land.

choices.text: Stop. Give them what you can spare.
choices.result: You give them five dollars and half the beans. Your own larder shrinks. Their oldest girl stops crying. You drive away lighter in every sense.

choices.text: Wave and keep rolling. You can't afford it.
choices.result: You tell yourself you can't help everyone. Your husband stares out the passenger window and says nothing the rest of the day.

choices.text: Stop. Help them flag a passing truck.
choices.result: You give them some food and wait with them until a truck stops. It costs you time and a little food — but not the cash you can't spare.

events.title: The Mojave at Night
events.text: The Mojave is brutal in daylight — radiators boil, tires blow, and the engine strains. Other migrants say to cross at night when it's cool. But night driving burns the headlights and frays nerves on unmarked roads.
trivia: Many Dust Bowl migrants crossed the Mojave Desert at night to avoid engine overheating and tire blowouts in the extreme daytime heat.
Route 66 through the Mojave was the main artery west — a two-lane road with few services for 150 miles.

choices.text: Cross by day. Stay together, drive careful.

outcomes.result: The radiator screams twice. You lose half a day nursing it and spend four dollars on roadside water. Made it, barely.
Brutal but passable. The kids sleep through the worst of it. The truck holds.

choices.text: Cross at night. Cooler, but harder to see.

outcomes.result: The dark is long but the engine stays cool. By morning you see the mountains and know California is close.
A rut you couldn't see in the dark buckles the front axle. Six dollars and most of a day to sort it roadside.

choices.text: Camp one day. Wait for a cooler stretch.
choices.result: You rest the engine under a scrub oak. The food goes fast sitting still, but the truck is steadier for the crossing.

events.title: The Border Brooms
events.text: California Highway Patrol has a checkpoint at the state line. They call them 'bum blockades.' An officer eyes the truck, eyes the family, and asks where you plan to work and whether you have money. He can turn you back or wave you through.
trivia: California set up border inspection stations in the 1930s that critics called 'bum blockades' — checkpoints designed to turn away destitute migrants, which many argued was unconstitutional.
Anti-Okie sentiment in California was widespread; some towns posted signs reading 'Okies and dogs not welcome.'

sageAdvice.name: California relief authority
sageAdvice.line: California can't feed the nation's poor. You want relief, go back where you came from.

choices.text: Show what cash you have. Stay calm.
choices.result: He counts the bills twice. Waves you through with a sneer. You let out a breath you've been holding since the Texas line.

choices.text: Tell him you have work waiting in Bakersfield.

outcomes.result: The name 'Bakersfield' does something. He waves you through. You hope the work is real.
He doesn't believe you. A 'fee' changes his mind. Five dollars you can't afford.

choices.text: Ask him on what legal authority he stops you.

outcomes.result: He hesitates. A car behind you honks. He waves you through, furious. You shook, but you asked.
He pulls you to the shoulder for an hour. 'Inspection.' You lose the afternoon and eight dollars in 'violations.' Worth it? You're still not sure.

events.title: The Camp or the Contractor
events.text: California, finally. Two roads from here: the labor contractor at the gate is offering work starting tomorrow — low wages, company housing, no questions. Down the road is Tom Collins's FSA camp, clean and run fair, but a waiting list and no guaranteed work. The family needs income today. Or a safe place to land.
trivia: Tom Collins managed the Arvin Federal Camp near Bakersfield, one of the few places in California where Okies were treated with dignity.
John Steinbeck visited Tom Collins's camp and used his notes to write The Grapes of Wrath.

sageAdvice.name: Tom Collins
sageAdvice.line: I can get your kids into school and your family into a clean tent. Work takes a little longer to arrange — but it's honest work.

sageAdvice.name: California agricultural labor contractor
sageAdvice.line: I need pickers by morning. Housing is included. Don't ask about the rate until you've seen the orchard.

choices.text: Take the contractor's offer. Family eats tomorrow.
choices.result: The wage is bad and the housing is a crowded tent in a ditch. But the children eat breakfast. You tell yourself it's temporary. For many families, it never was.

choices.text: Go to Collins's camp. Wait for honest work.

choices.result: It keeps the family fed but apart. Evenings are short and tired. The distance feels like more than miles.

events.title: The Relief Line — weeks or months later, depending on the road taken

text.default: You stand in a county relief line outside Barstow. The woman ahead of you has an Oklahoma accent and does not meet anyone's eyes. What you know is that you made the choice and you are the one who made it, and on the nights when the children cough from the roadside dust, that knowledge sits in you like a stone that is also, somehow, a compass.

sages.name: Hugh Hammond Bennett
sages.title: Chief, Soil Conservation Service
sages.bio: Hugh Hammond Bennett spent his career warning that American topsoil was being destroyed by careless farming. When the Dust Bowl hit, he became the loudest voice for federal soil conservation — and the man most responsible for creating the Soil Conservation Service in 1935.
sages.greeting: You're camped roadside in the Texas Panhandle when a dusty federal car pulls over. A big man climbs out and looks at the drifts against your truck like he's seen it a thousand times.
sages.advice: "This land didn't fail you. It was used up and left bare — wheat planted fence to fence, no windbreaks, no cover. The dust is the bill for thirty years of that."

question.question: What farming practice most directly caused the grasslands to become vulnerable to the Dust Bowl?
choices: Farmers planted too many trees, blocking natural wind patterns
Plowing up native grassland removed the deep roots that held the soil in place
Irrigation flooded the topsoil and washed it into rivers
Cattle ranchers burned pastures to encourage new growth
question.explanation: The Southern Plains' native grasses had deep root systems that anchored the soil against wind. When farmers plowed millions of acres for wheat — especially during the boom years of World War One — that root structure was destroyed. When drought came and crops dried up, there was nothing to hold the soil.
question.teksRef: 8.29(A) — Environmental and economic causes of the Dust Bowl and the Great Depression

sages.name: Dorothea Lange
sages.title: FSA Documentary Photographer
sages.bio: Dorothea Lange worked for the Farm Security Administration, driving the back roads of the Southwest to photograph tenant farmers and migrants. Her image 'Migrant Mother' — taken in 1936 — became the defining face of the Depression and helped mobilize public support for federal relief.
sages.greeting: She's parked beside an irrigation ditch, camera on her lap, watching families file into a pea-pickers' camp. She asks if she can photograph your truck.
sages.advice: "People in cities don't know what this road looks like. When they see it — really see it — they ask their senators for something better. Your face is an argument I can make."

question.question: Which New Deal agency hired Dorothea Lange to photograph the Dust Bowl migration?
choices: The Works Progress Administration (WPA)
The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC)
The Farm Security Administration (FSA)
The Agricultural Adjustment Administration (AAA)
question.explanation: The Farm Security Administration employed photographers including Dorothea Lange, Walker Evans, and others to document rural poverty across America. The images they produced helped build public and congressional support for New Deal relief programs.
question.teksRef: 8.29(B) — New Deal programs and their relationship to the Dust Bowl migration

sages.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
sages.title: President of the United States
sages.bio: Franklin Roosevelt took office in 1933 with one in four Americans unemployed and the farm economy in collapse. His New Deal created dozens of federal programs — the AAA, the FSA, the CCC, the WPA — attempting to stabilize agriculture, put people to work, and provide a floor of relief for the poorest Americans.
sages.greeting: A radio crackles at a filling station. The president's voice comes through — a Fireside Chat. The attendant turns it up. You sit on the running board and listen.
sages.advice: "We have a rendezvous with destiny — but for families on this road, destiny looks like a tent and a wage that won't cover the week. The programs we've built are the floor, not the ceiling."

question.question: What did Roosevelt's Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA) do that hurt many tenant farmers and sharecroppers?
choices: It banned tenant farming in drought-affected states
It paid landowners to reduce crops, allowing them to evict tenants whose labor was no longer needed
It forced farmers to sell their land to the federal government at low prices
It created a new tax on farm equipment that small farmers could not afford
question.explanation: The AAA paid landowners to take land out of production to raise crop prices. Many landlords used those federal payments to buy tractors — which could farm more land with fewer people — and evicted the tenant farmers they no longer needed. The New Deal's farm programs sometimes accelerated the displacement they were meant to relieve.

It paid landowners to reduce crops, letting them evict tenants they no longer needed

It banned sharecropping in drought counties
eventTrivia.fact: AAA payments went to landowners, who used the money to buy tractors and dismissed the tenant families whose labor was now redundant.

The Civilian Conservation Corps
The Farm Security Administration

eventTrivia.fact: The FSA built and operated a small number of sanitary migrant camps in California. Tom Collins managed the Arvin camp near Bakersfield, one of the most well-known.

eventTrivia.question: Why did tenant farming families often have no savings when the bank foreclosed?
choices: Banks charged tenant farmers extra fees to open accounts
Crop prices had fallen so low that harvests barely covered rent and debt, leaving nothing
The federal government taxed tenant farmers at higher rates than landowners
Tenant farmers were legally prohibited from owning savings accounts in Oklahoma
eventTrivia.fact: Crop prices collapsed in the late 1920s and stayed low through the Depression. A family that owed rent and seed costs on a bad harvest ended each year deeper in debt, not richer.

eventTrivia.question: What made the drought of the 1930s worse than earlier dry spells on the Plains?
choices: Temperatures were several degrees higher than any previous drought
The topsoil had been plowed bare, so when it dried it turned to blowing dust instead of holding
Farmers had cut down all the trees, causing permanent climate change
Underground aquifers had been pumped dry by irrigation
eventTrivia.fact: Earlier Plains droughts had struck grassland that bounced back. By the 1930s, the grass was gone and the bare soil simply blew away — turning a drought into a sustained environmental disaster.

eventTrivia.question: What was a 'labor contractor' in California's agricultural economy?
choices: A federal official who set minimum wages for farm workers
A middleman who recruited and controlled migrant workers, often paying below-market wages
A union organizer who negotiated contracts for pickers
A bank officer who made loans to migrants for farm equipment
eventTrivia.fact: Labor contractors recruited desperate migrants, often promising better conditions than they delivered. They controlled housing and work assignments, making it difficult for families to negotiate or leave.

eventTrivia.question: What was 'Migrant Mother,' and why did it matter?
choices: A relief pamphlet distributed at California border checkpoints
A Dorothea Lange photograph that became a symbol of Depression-era suffering and spurred relief efforts
A government program providing housing loans to displaced farm families
A novel about the Dust Bowl migration that preceded The Grapes of Wrath
eventTrivia.fact: Lange photographed Florence Owens Thompson and her children at a pea-pickers' camp in 1936. The image was published nationally and helped accelerate federal food relief to California migrant camps.

eventTrivia.question: What primary source of income did Oklahoma Panhandle tenant families lose first when the Dust Bowl hit?
choices: Livestock sales
Wheat and cotton crops
Timber rights
Factory wages
eventTrivia.fact: Panhandle families depended almost entirely on cash crops — wheat especially. When drought killed the harvest and prices were already low from the Depression, the crop income that paid rent and debt simply vanished.

eventTrivia.question: What did Tom Collins's FSA camp at Arvin offer that private labor camps did not?
choices: Guaranteed wages set by the federal government
Sanitary facilities, a school, and treatment with basic dignity
Free transportation back to Oklahoma for families who wanted to return
Priority hiring contracts with California fruit growers
eventTrivia.fact: Collins's camp had running water, toilets, a school for children, and self-governance for residents — conditions that stood in sharp contrast to the ditch-bank camps run by private growers.

eventTrivia.question: Why did many Great Plains families load trucks rather than trains when they migrated west?
choices: Railroads refused to sell tickets to Oklahomans after 1933
A truck let families carry their belongings and stop for work along the way
The federal government provided gasoline vouchers to migrant families with trucks
Train fare to California was more expensive than buying a truck
eventTrivia.fact: A truck was slow and unreliable but gave the family flexibility — they could carry what they owned, stop to pick crops for cash, and arrive in California with at least a vehicle and their household goods.

data.historicalContext: Between 1930 and 1940, an estimated 3.5 million people left the Great Plains — roughly 400,000 of them ending up in California. They came to be called Okies regardless of their state of origin. California's agricultural valleys absorbed tens of thousands of these families into a labor system that paid poverty wages and housed people in roadside ditches. The federal FSA camps run by men like Tom Collins offered a small number of families something better. The Dust Bowl itself was not ended by migration or policy — it ended when the rains returned in 1939. By then, the Great Plains had lost an estimated 850 million tons of topsoil, and the families who had sharecropped that land were scattered from California to Oregon, starting over with nothing.

verdict.good: You made it to California, and you brought something with you the road could not strip away. You stopped for the family on the shoulder. You asked the officer on what authority he stopped you. You chose the camp over the quick money. None of it was safe, and some of it cost you. The Dust Bowl was not solved by the people who showed up on the right side of those choices — the rains came back in 1939 on their own schedule, indifferent to human decency. But the families who survived with their dignity intact survived as people, not just as bodies that made it west. That was not nothing. In 1935 it was almost everything.
verdict.bad: You made it to California. Every choice that got you there was the choice that looked after you first and let someone else carry the cost. The family on the shoulder — you drove past. The contractor's low wage — you took it without a word and told yourself you had no choice. You did. The road from Oklahoma to California in 1935 was a gauntlet that stripped people down to what they actually were. You found out what you were. You arrived. You were fed. The woman in the ditch with three kids and a cracked axle is still in the ditch. The math worked out for you.
verdict.indifferent: You made it. You kept your head down, took the offer that was in front of you, and waited for the hard choices to resolve themselves without your input. The border officer waved you through. The contractor had work. The road was long and you stayed on it. The Dust Bowl displaced 3.5 million people from the Great Plains and scattered them into labor camps and ditch-bank tents across California. That happened around you. You passed through it. When it was over you couldn't have said clearly what you stood for, because you never had to decide. The road asked nothing of you, because you offered nothing to ask.

data.reviewSummary:
In the summer of 1935, tenant farming families across the Oklahoma Panhandle faced a compounding disaster: years of drought had killed the crops, falling crop prices meant harvests no longer covered rent and debt, and the native grassland that once held the topsoil had been plowed bare for wheat. When it dried out, the soil simply blew away. Hugh Hammond Bennett, the chief of the new Soil Conservation Service, had spent years explaining that mass plowing had destroyed the deep-rooted grasses that anchored the Plains against wind — turning ordinary drought into a sustained environmental catastrophe that stripped an estimated 850 million tons of topsoil from the land.

For families who left, the route west meant loading a truck with what the household could carry, scraping together cash from sold furniture and livestock, and following Route 66 through Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and across the Mojave Desert into California. Many stopped along the way to pick cotton or sugar beets for day wages — the only way to keep gas in the tank and food in the larder. Labor contractors at crossroads recruited desperate families with promises of work, then delivered low piece-rate wages and cramped company housing, with little room to negotiate or leave.

At the California border, state patrol checkpoints — called 'bum blockades' by critics — turned back destitute migrants, a practice many legal scholars considered unconstitutional. Once inside California, families entered an agricultural labor system that offered poverty wages and ditch-bank camps as standard housing.

Federal photographers working for the Farm Security Administration, including Dorothea Lange, documented these conditions and distributed the images to build public and congressional support for relief programs. Roosevelt's New Deal created programs like the FSA, which funded a small number of clean migrant camps. Tom Collins managed one of the most notable at Arvin, near Bakersfield, where residents had sanitary facilities, a school for their children, and basic dignity — conditions that stood apart from the private growers' camps. But the AAA, another New Deal program, sometimes made displacement worse: it paid landowners to reduce crop production, allowing them to evict tenant families whose labor was no longer needed and replace them with tractors. The Dust Bowl did not end until the rains returned in 1939.

data.title: CORPS OF DISCOVERY
data.subtitle: St. Louis to the Pacific, 1804–1806
data.introBody: Spring, 1804. St. Louis, Missouri. President Jefferson has sent you west to map the Louisiana Purchase, find a river route to the Pacific, and make contact with Native nations. Outfit your party carefully — there are no supply posts beyond the Missouri.
data.trailFeedOpener: May 1804: the keelboat pushes off from Camp Dubois and noses into the Missouri current.

events.title: The Mandan Villages
events.text: You reach the Mandan villages on the upper Missouri and make winter camp nearby. The Mandans offer trade and food — but how you treat them will shape every Native encounter ahead.
trivia: The Corps spent the winter of 1804–1805 at Fort Mandan, near present-day Bismarck, North Dakota.
Sacagawea and her husband Toussaint Charbonneau were hired at Fort Mandan as interpreters.

sageAdvice.name: Red Feather
sageAdvice.line: A gift given honestly opens more doors than a soldier's rifle.

sageAdvice.name: Sergeant Ordway
sageAdvice.line: These villages fed us through the coldest winter. We owe them respect.

choices.text: Trade fairly and share medical knowledge.
choices.result: The Mandans welcome you warmly, share food, and help you hire Sacagawea as interpreter.

choices.text: Trade only for what you need, stay distant.
choices.result: You get supplies but little trust. The winter feels long and cold.

choices.text: Demand provisions, citing Jefferson's authority.
choices.result: The Mandans comply but word spreads upriver. Future nations will be wary.

events.title: Portage Around the Great Falls
events.text: The Great Falls of the Missouri block your boats completely. An eighteen-mile portage over sharp rock and prickly pear awaits — it will take weeks and test every man.
trivia: The portage around the Great Falls took about three weeks in June 1805.
Lewis described the Great Falls as the most magnificent sight he had ever witnessed.

choices.text: Build wagons from cottonwood and push hard.

outcomes.result: The axles crack but hold. Three brutal weeks and you're past the falls.
A wagon collapses on the worst stretch. Journals soaked. The men are spent.

choices.text: Slow careful portage — record everything.
choices.result: The crossing takes longer but Lewis fills pages with detailed observations of the falls and plains.

choices.text: Leave the heavy keelboat behind.
choices.result: Lighter loads help — but losing that cargo hurts. You'll feel it in the mountains.

events.title: The Shoshone and the Horses
events.text: The rivers have ended. The Rockies rise ahead and you need horses. The Shoshone chief, Cameahwait, has horses — but he has no reason to trust strangers with guns.
trivia: Sacagawea recognized Cameahwait as her brother, which helped broker the horse trade.
Without Shoshone horses, the Corps could not have crossed the Bitterroot Mountains.

sageAdvice.name: Sacagawea
sageAdvice.line: Let me speak. He is my brother. Trust must come before horses.

choices.text: Let Sacagawea lead the negotiation.
choices.result: Sacagawea's reunion with her brother Cameahwait moves both sides. You ride out with horses and a guide.

choices.text: Offer rifles and trade goods for horses.

outcomes.result: Cameahwait trades but looks worried. A long silence follows.
Displaying rifles frightens the camp. They scatter. The trade collapses.

choices.text: Wait and observe. Let them approach you.
choices.result: Days pass. Provisions drop. Eventually a deal is made, but time is lost.

events.title: Into the Bitterroots
events.text: The Bitterroot Mountains are the hardest miles of the entire journey. Snow, steep trails, and exhausted horses. Every extra push risks men and mounts.
events.leaveText: Make camp. Rest until the pass clears.

attempts.buttonText: Push one more ridge before dark.
attempts.successText: You gain a ridge. The Nez Perce trail comes into view — a real path west.
attempts.failureText: Ice and loose rock. Two horses slip. Medicine kit damaged.

attempts.successText: You crest the summit by moonlight. The Columbia basin glitters far below.
attempts.failureText: A man collapses with cold and exhaustion. You must camp and treat him.

events.title: Chinook Nations on the Columbia
events.text: You've reached the lower Columbia and the Chinook people, who control river trade here. They are skilled traders — and they know you need their knowledge to reach the Pacific.
trivia: The Chinook people had extensive trade networks along the Columbia River long before European contact.
Lewis and Clark voted as a group on where to build their Pacific coast winter camp — including York, an enslaved man, and Sacagawea.

choices.text: Trade honestly — blue beads for canoe passage.
choices.result: Blue beads are prized here. The Chinook guide you through the rapids and share dried salmon.

choices.text: Record their trade goods, then demand passage.
choices.result: The Chinook refuse to help and word spreads downriver. The Corps reaches the coast exhausted and distrusted.

choices.text: Camp and wait for another band to help.

outcomes.result: A smaller band arrives and offers limited help. You push through slowly.
A chief comes to camp and offers information freely. Patience paid.

sages.advice: "You are to observe the soil, the rivers, the minerals, and above all the manners of the Native nations. Treat them as friends. Their goodwill is worth more than any map."

sages.advice: "A woman and a child do not travel with a war party. The nations we meet will know this. Speak through me and speak true."

She served as interpreter, identified western plants and terrain, and helped show peaceful intent

data.historicalContext: The Lewis and Clark Expedition (1804–1806) traveled over 8,000 miles round trip. The Corps reached the Pacific Ocean in November 1805 and returned to St. Louis in September 1806. Their maps and journals became the foundation for American westward expansion across the 1800s. Their encounters with dozens of Native nations — some peaceful, some tense — set patterns for U.S.-Native diplomacy that followed. Sacagawea, York, and the Shoshone, Mandan, and Nez Perce peoples were all essential to the expedition's survival.

verdict.good: You led with honesty — traded fairly, listened to Sacagawea, treated Native nations as people rather than obstacles. It cost you time and supplies. The expedition succeeded anyway, the way it actually succeeded in 1806: not through force, but because enough nations chose to help. Lewis and Clark came home. You earned that homecoming.
verdict.bad: You took what you needed and called it diplomacy. Every shortcut worked — until it didn't — and someone else paid the price. The Corps made it to the Pacific. But the goodwill Jefferson asked you to build, the trust that was supposed to outlast the journey? You burned most of it. History remembers the expedition as a triumph. It also remembers how it treated the people who made it possible.
verdict.indifferent: You kept the boat moving and let the hard choices pass. You were there for every river crossing, every mountain, every village — and you offered nothing when it asked something of you. The expedition reached the Pacific. Lewis and Clark came home and changed American history. You were present for all of it and left no mark on any of it. The land was mapped. The people you met were changed forever by what followed. You kept your head down and passed through.

data.reviewSummary:
In 1804, President Thomas Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark west to explore the Louisiana Purchase — a vast territory the United States had bought from France in 1803, doubling the country's size. Jefferson's goals were clear: map a river route to the Pacific Ocean, document plants, animals, and geography, and make peaceful contact with Native nations along the way.

The Corps of Discovery set out from Camp Dubois near St. Louis in May 1804, pushing up the Missouri River. That fall they reached the Mandan villages on the upper Missouri, near present-day Bismarck, North Dakota, and built Fort Mandan for the winter. There they hired Toussaint Charbonneau and his Shoshone wife Sacagawea as interpreters. Sacagawea proved essential to the expedition's survival — she interpreted Native languages, identified edible plants and familiar terrain, and her presence with her infant son Jean Baptiste signaled to every nation they encountered that the Corps was a peaceful mission, not a war party.

In the summer of 1805 the expedition portaged around the Great Falls of the Missouri — an eighteen-mile carry over sharp rock that took nearly three weeks. Beyond the falls, the rivers ended and the Rocky Mountains rose ahead. The Corps needed horses to cross the Bitterroot range. Sacagawea recognized the Shoshone chief Cameahwait as her own brother, and that reunion made the horse trade possible. Without Shoshone horses, the Bitterroot crossing could not have been made.

The Corps reached the Pacific Ocean in November 1805 and wintered at Fort Clatsop. They returned to St. Louis in September 1806. The maps and journals Clark and Lewis brought back gave Americans their first detailed knowledge of the West and directly encouraged and guided the westward expansion that followed through the rest of the 1800s. The expedition's interactions with the Mandan, Shoshone, Nez Perce, Chinook, and dozens of other nations set early patterns for U.S.-Native relations — both the respectful exchanges and the conflicts that came after.
